evidence.title: Paper craft workshop kit assembly
evidence.beneficiary: Workshop participants and the two volunteer kit assemblers
evidence.valued_outcome: Every participant receives a complete kit matching the assigned paper craft pattern before the workshop begins.
evidence.success_measure: All 60 kits are ready within 90 minutes, with at most one kit requiring correction at distribution.

hard_constraints.text: Each kit must retain the specified quantities and paper dimensions for its assigned pattern.
Assembly uses exactly two volunteers for at most 90 minutes.
All work must fit on the existing 180-by-75-centimetre table.
Use existing paper envelopes and supplies; no new equipment or purchases.

evidence.incumbent: Volunteers assemble envelopes individually by taking materials from shared trays, then place completed kits in a stack. Three patterns use overlapping materials in different quantities. Two existing partial mechanisms are coloured tray tags identifying material types and a displayed completed sample kit showing the contents of each pattern. One volunteer checks finished envelopes when assembly stops.

observations.text: Synthetic assembly sheet: 60 kits took 86 minutes, followed by an eleven-minute check.
Synthetic contents audit: seven kits lacked one item; five omissions concerned materials shared by multiple patterns.
Synthetic movement tally: volunteers reached across one another 38 times during the sampled session.
Synthetic small-batch record: twelve kits assembled with materials loose beside each volunteer had no omissions and took 15 minutes, awkwardly challenging reliance on shared tagged trays.
Synthetic supply record: one paper colour ran short after 43 kits; usable sheets remained in an unopened packet under the table.
Synthetic sample-use tally: volunteers consulted the displayed samples twice during the 60-kit session.
Synthetic distribution notes: three participants exchanged envelopes because their assigned patterns were not apparent from the exterior.

unknowns: Whether the small batch used the same pattern mixture.
Whether omissions arise during picking or envelope filling.
How much table area opened supply packets occupy.
resources: Existing tagged trays and sample kits.
Paper envelopes, pencils and the specified craft materials.
changeable_assumptions: Each volunteer completes an entire kit before starting another.
Materials remain in shared trays throughout assembly.
Contents checking happens after all envelopes are filled.
evidence.provenance: Entirely authored synthetic fixture. All named sheets, audits, records and notes are supplied stipulations, not field observations or tested effects.

reports.concern: Complete contents and correct pattern at distribution
reports.claim: Assuming pattern exchanges reflect unclear envelope identity, S2:O7 implies distribution clarity matters alongside completeness, while S2:O2 shows contents alone remain unreliable.
assumptions: Unclear envelope identity caused the exchanges.

reports.concern: Shared material handling within time and space limits
reports.claim: Assuming crossed reaches interrupt picking, S2:O3 and S2:O4 suggest material access may contribute to omissions; distributing materials could also consume table area constrained by S2:C3.
assumptions: Crossed reaches interrupt picking.
Distributed materials consume additional table area.

reports.concern: Comparison between the small batch and full session
reports.claim: Assuming pattern mixtures differ, S2:O4 cannot attribute its fewer omissions to loose materials; S2:O1 includes a separate check, further limiting direct speed comparison.
assumptions: Pattern mixtures may differ.
The small-batch timing may exclude equivalent checking.

evidence.tension: Distribution evidence expands the valued outcome beyond contents; operational inference favours attention to material access under tight space limits; evidence interpretation withholds the comparative claim that supports that emphasis. No implication establishes which change would meet the deadline.

families.signature: Overlapping pattern requirements can cause memory interference: an assembler may carry one pattern's count into another. Omissions should cluster at pattern transitions or shared materials, with the picked quantity matching a different pattern's requirement.
families.assumptions: Volunteers switch patterns and rely on memory. Five shared-material omissions are consistent with interference but could also reflect filling losses or shortages; transition and quantity records are absent.

families.signature: Shared-tray access can create movement contention. Cross-reaching should coincide with pauses, interrupted counts or material displacement, and kits assembled during those interruptions may take longer or contain more errors.
families.assumptions: The 38 reaches interfere with work rather than being harmless movement. The tally supplies no duration or kit-level linkage, so it cannot quantify delay or establish an omission cause.

families.signature: Local material visibility may reduce search and picking mistakes, but small-batch success may instead reflect an easier pattern mix or lower workload. Error and time differences should follow comparable patterns and quantities before being attributed to material placement.
families.assumptions: Loose materials are distinguishable and fit the table. Twelve kits provide limited exposure; their pattern mixture, preparation time and full-session feasibility are unknown.

families.signature: Visible stock depletion can mimic a true shortage when reserve supplies are hidden. Picking should pause or skip a required colour after the tray empties despite remaining usable inventory, with availability restored when the reserve is discovered.
families.assumptions: The unopened packet contains the required colour and dimensions. The record indicates usable sheets but does not connect depletion to omitted items or measure interruption time.

families.signature: Deferred checking creates a serial work tail and allows errors to accumulate before detection. Total readiness time exceeds filling time, and corrections discovered at the end can extend the tail further; repeated defects may span many completed envelopes.
families.assumptions: The eleven-minute check is additional elapsed work within the stipulated assembly window. Check staffing, correction time and detection completeness are unspecified; the contents audit may be separate from that check.

families.signature: An envelope's contents can be complete while its assigned pattern is unclear during distribution. Exchanges should arise from identity ambiguity rather than missing contents, with a correct kit initially reaching the wrong pattern recipient.
families.assumptions: Participants' assignments are stable and exchanges reflect exterior ambiguity. Three exchanges do not prove incomplete kits; their treatment as corrections under the success measure is unspecified.

openings.claim: Material access may cause picking omissions, but the small-batch comparison does not establish this. Evaluate a bounded probe, not a proven intervention for participants and the two assemblers.
openings.delta: Compare shared tagged trays with limited loose materials beside each volunteer while matching patterns, envelope identification and checking.
openings.prediction: With matched patterns and equivalent checks, loose access reduces picking omissions and crossed reaches without increasing total audited assembly time or exceeding table space.
openings.rival_prediction: The nearest alternative is that pattern mix or omitted checking explains the small-batch advantage: matching these removes the advantage, with omissions persisting during filling despite fewer reaches.
openings.defeat: Equal or more picking omissions under loose access, worse fully audited time, or inability to fit its supplies on the existing table defeats the proposed advantage in this probe; zero errors in both arms is inconclusive.
openings.probe: Use the first twelve production kits as six matched pairs, two pairs per pattern, one kit per layout. Balance layout order and volunteer assignments. Pencil the assigned pattern on every envelope. Tally reaches and compare picked contents before filling with contents after filling against the specified sample; record corrections and all checking, setup and restocking time. Keep every layout within the existing table and count everything inside the same two-volunteer, 90-minute production budget. Use existing envelopes, pencils and materials only.
assumptions: Enough existing material can be staged for the bounded comparison; usable quantities are unverified.
The limited loose layout can fit; measure before starting it.
Inline observation and checking are feasible for the two volunteers without extra assistance.

evidence.decision: Run only the bounded comparison that fits the measured table and remaining production budget. Its observations can change which mechanism merits attention; they cannot establish that all 60 correct-pattern kits will be ready within 90 minutes with at most one distribution correction. Current evidence is synthetic stipulation, not tested benefit.

unresolved.issue: Envelope ambiguity may cause exchanges; identification is held constant here, so its effect remains untested.
Full-run restocking, footprint and total checking time remain unproven.

openings.claim: Shared material access may contribute to omissions, but the synthetic small batch does not establish this cause or a deadline-saving intervention.
openings.delta: Compare shared trays with materials beside each volunteer while holding pattern mixture, quantities, identity marking and checking constant.
openings.prediction: With equivalent patterns and checks, local access produces fewer crossed reaches and omissions without increasing total checked-kit time.
openings.rival_prediction: Different pattern mixtures or checking exposure explain the small batch; matching these removes its omission and timing advantage even if crossed reaches decrease.
openings.defeat: A matched comparison finds equal or worse omissions or checked-kit time with local access; inability to fit the materials on the existing table defeats that layout's feasibility.
openings.probe: Using existing supplies, tally sheets and pencils, first count stock and measure both layouts within the table boundary. If either cannot fit, stop that comparison. Within a single 90-minute budget including setup and checks, exactly two volunteers assemble two matched six-kit blocks, reversing access order across volunteers. Pencil the assigned pattern on every envelope and check specified quantities and dimensions before closing in both conditions. Record reaches, omissions, elapsed time and distribution identity errors. Do not extrapolate twelve kits to sixty.
assumptions: The required stock is sufficient; an unopened packet alone does not verify this.
Both layouts can fit the table; occupied supply area is unknown.
A matched pattern mixture can be constructed.
Pencil pattern identification may prevent exchanges, but its benefit is untested.

evidence.decision: Converge on a bounded matched comparison, subject to stock and table-fit verification. Its intended fit preserves all constraints without relaxation; actual feasibility and intervention success remain unproven. Participants and both assemblers still require all sixty complete, correctly assigned kits within ninety minutes and at most one distribution correction. All evidence is authored synthetic stipulation; no tested benefit or stakeholder agreement is established.

unresolved.issue: Picking versus filling as the omission source remains unresolved.
Neither the comparison nor exterior marking establishes full-run throughput or distribution accuracy.

openings.claim: Personal loose-material staging may reduce picking omissions by reducing crossed reaches; O4 does not yet establish this mechanism.
openings.delta: Replace the unmatched small-batch comparison with matched pattern counts, equal checking and counterbalanced volunteer exposure.
openings.prediction: With identical pattern mixtures and audits, personal staging produces fewer crossed reaches and fewer missing items before checking, without increasing total setup, assembly and checking time.
openings.rival_prediction: The nearest alternative is that O4 benefited from its pattern mixture or unequal checking. Matched mixtures and equivalent audits remove its omission and timing advantage even if reaches decline.
openings.defeat: Personal staging reduces reaches but leaves omissions unchanged or higher, or its setup and checking erase the time advantage; inability to fit defeats this layout's feasibility.
openings.probe: Use twelve of the sixty required kits: each volunteer assembles one kit of each pattern under each layout, in opposite layout orders. Preserve specified contents. Use exactly two volunteers, existing materials, and only the existing table; attempt loose staging only if it fits. Count the probe and corrections inside the overall ninety-minute limit. Pencil assigned patterns on all twelve envelopes as a common distribution safeguard, not a tested benefit.
assumptions: Both layouts fit with existing supplies; this must be checked before staging.
The required assignment includes enough kits of each pattern for matching.
A twelve-kit comparison can reveal a decision-changing difference; a tie remains inconclusive.

evidence.decision: Proceed only with the bounded matched probe after its feasibility checks. Its guarded design preserves hard constraints; no supplied synthetic stipulation proves the eventual intervention delivers complete, correctly assigned kits to participants within ninety minutes with at most one distribution correction, or reduces volunteer burden.

unresolved.issue: Picking versus filling failures and small-batch comparability remain untested.
Envelope identification is independently required; pencilling patterns has no tested distribution outcome.
Supply continuity, table occupancy and sixty-kit completion remain unproven.

openings.claim: Shared access may contribute to omissions, but the stipulated small batch does not establish that adjacent materials improve full-session performance.
openings.delta: Replace reliance on the uncontrolled small-batch comparison with a bounded comparison that localizes omissions and measures checking time.
openings.prediction: With the same pattern mixture and checking procedure, adjacent material allotments produce fewer crossed reaches and fewer picking omissions than shared trays.
openings.rival_prediction: The small batch benefited from an easier pattern mixture or different checking; matching those factors removes its omission advantage even if crossed reaches decrease.
openings.defeat: Matched batches show equally frequent or more picking omissions with adjacent allotments despite fewer crossed reaches, or omissions arise mainly during filling.
openings.probe: Using exactly two volunteers and existing supplies, compare two twelve-kit batches with identical pattern counts and quantities. Use shared trays for one and small adjacent allotments for the other; reverse order in any later replication. Pencil the assigned pattern on envelopes in both batches. Record picking versus filling errors, crossed reaches, replenishment, and setup, assembly and equivalent checking time. Include all opened supplies within the existing table; stop before exceeding 90 minutes or if either layout cannot fit.
assumptions: The bounded comparison evaluates a probe, not a proven intervention capable of delivering all 60 kits.
Adjacent allotments may not fit alongside supplies; their feasibility remains unconfirmed.
One ordered comparison cannot exclude learning or fatigue effects.

evidence.decision: Converge on the stipulated failure: assembly plus checking totals 97 minutes, seven kits are incomplete, and exterior pattern identity is unclear. Test material access under controlled conditions while making pattern identity explicit in both arms. Preserve the original goal for participants and assemblers: 60 complete, correctly assigned kits within 90 minutes, with at most one correction. No supplied report establishes an intervention meeting it.

Pattern markings and access changes have no tested distribution or full-session outcome.

evidence.title: Public library hold pickup at the evening desk
evidence.beneficiary: Readers collecting reserved books and the evening desk clerk
evidence.valued_outcome: A reader receives the correct available hold promptly, without exposing another reader's identity.
evidence.success_measure: At least 95% of available-hold pickups finish within two minutes during the stipulated evening window; no wrong-reader handoffs.

hard_constraints.text: Only the existing evening clerk may perform handoffs; no additional staffing.
Reader names and contact details must remain behind the desk.
Use the existing two shelves and one return cart; do not add furniture.
Daily preparation must fit within ten clerk-minutes.

evidence.incumbent: The clerk retrieves books from two behind-desk shelves arranged alphabetically by reader surname. Two existing partial mechanisms are surname divider cards, which narrow the search region, and a daily paper exception slip, which records holds temporarily elsewhere. The slip is completed before evening opening. Newly arrived books can remain on the return cart until the next shelving pass.

observations.text: Synthetic timing log: 12 of 40 available-hold encounters exceeded two minutes; eight of those included a second search location.
Synthetic shelf audit: six of 70 books were placed under the surname of another household member.
Synthetic exception-slip sample: four of 16 recorded locations no longer matched the book location by evening.
Synthetic cart timing sample: ten pickups of newly arrived books still on the cart each finished within one minute, challenging the assumption that shelving necessarily accelerates retrieval.
Synthetic desk count: 24 of 40 encounters occurred in the same 25-minute interval.
Synthetic clerk diary: preparation took eight minutes on the sampled day; corrections after opening took six more minutes.
Synthetic reader interviews: five of eight delayed readers said uncertainty about whether their hold was present bothered them more than the walk to the desk.

unknowns: Whether household-name mismatches explain second-location searches.
How arrival volume and book size affect the cart sample.
Whether the interview sample represents evening readers.
resources: Existing divider cards, paper and pencils.
Two shelves and one return cart.
changeable_assumptions: Surname determines the primary storage address.
Location exceptions are recorded once before opening.
All arrivals should eventually enter the same shelf order.
evidence.provenance: Entirely authored synthetic fixture. Named logs, audits, diaries and interviews are supplied stipulations, not field observations or tested effects.

reports.concern: Certainty about availability during a delayed pickup
reports.claim: Assuming the interview sample represents evening readers, S1:O7 implies that an accurate availability answer could matter even when retrieval remains slow.
assumptions: The eight interviewed readers represent evening demand.

reports.concern: Reliable location records within preparation capacity
reports.claim: Assuming stale exception locations cause second searches, S1:O1 and S1:O3 imply location upkeep deserves priority; S1:O6 suggests that priority may exceed the preparation allowance.
assumptions: Stale locations cause second searches.
Corrections require clerk time comparable to the sampled day.

reports.concern: Meaning of the faster cart sample
reports.claim: Assuming cart pickups differ in arrival recency or volume, S1:O4 cannot establish that cart storage improves retrieval; it weakens any unconditional claim that shelf order is faster.
assumptions: The cart sample may differ from shelf pickups in recency or volume.

evidence.tension: Reader evidence points toward availability certainty; operational inference points toward costly location upkeep; the cart sample questions the storage assumption while leaving its causal interpretation unsettled. These implications compete for the same limited clerk time.

families.signature: Household-name ambiguity can separate the lookup name from the storage name. If causal, delayed encounters and second-location searches should disproportionately involve books filed under a different household member, with retrieval occurring only after trying that alternate name.
families.assumptions: The surname audit and timing encounters concern comparable holds. Their supplied counts are unlinked, so the six mismatches cannot yet explain any particular delay; mistaken placement need not cause a wrong-reader handoff.

families.signature: A location record can become stale when a book moves after the exception slip is completed. The signature is a recorded location searched unsuccessfully, followed by finding the book at a later destination, with movement occurring between recording and retrieval.
families.assumptions: Books move during the day and clerks consult the slip. Four inaccurate entries establish disagreement, but neither its cause nor its contribution to delay is supplied.

families.signature: Retrieval cost may follow search-set size, visibility and handling rather than whether a book is shelved. A small, recent cart load could produce shorter searches than a crowded alphabetical region; comparable loads should expose whether that relationship persists.
families.assumptions: The cart sample may have fewer books or easier-to-handle sizes. Ten fast pickups lack a matched shelf comparison and do not establish a scalable cart advantage.

families.signature: Arrival bursts can generate a queue when demand temporarily exceeds one clerk's service capacity. Waiting should rise within the concentrated interval even for correctly located books, while the clerk's actual retrieval durations could remain stable.
families.assumptions: Encounter timing may include waiting, but the timing definition is unspecified. Concentrated arrivals alone do not prove overload without service durations and arrival ordering.

families.signature: Preparation defects may shift work into opening hours. Corrections should follow mismatches or obsolete location records and consume clerk time otherwise available for handoffs, potentially lengthening subsequent waits.
families.assumptions: Diary corrections are relevant to holds. Their causes and overlap with peak demand are unknown; whether all corrections count as daily preparation is not specified.

families.signature: Uncertainty about availability may increase perceived burden independently of physical retrieval time. Readers with equally long encounters could report different dissatisfaction according to whether they knew the hold was present.
families.assumptions: Interview statements reflect experience, but eight delayed readers may be unrepresentative. Reduced uncertainty alone would not establish the two-minute target or correct handoff.

openings.claim: Private location updates at book moves may improve both retrieval and availability certainty more than an availability answer alone.
openings.delta: Compare availability-only answers with move-triggered exception-slip updates; keep surname dividers and identity checks.
openings.prediction: For comparable displaced holds, updates reduce second searches and pickup time; verified availability answers reduce reported uncertainty in both conditions.
openings.rival_prediction: Availability-only answers reduce uncertainty equally, while updates add work without improving retrieval because household-name errors or queues dominate.
openings.defeat: Updates consume the preparation allowance without reducing second searches or pickup duration.
openings.probe: Clerk performs a small paired rehearsal of the same displaced holds using existing paper and timing sheet: answer-only versus updated locations. Alternate order; record search locations, identity-check errors, elapsed time and preparation minutes. Count all preparation against ten minutes and stop at the cap. Reader uncertainty effects require a later authorized reader comparison.
assumptions: A rehearsal can fit alongside ordinary preparation within ten clerk-minutes.
Matched rehearsal searches approximate evening retrieval; reader representativeness remains unknown.

openings.claim: Does cart speed survive matching arrival recency, book size and search load?
openings.delta: Treat cart storage as a competing retrieval explanation, rather than accepting shelving superiority.
openings.prediction: With location records equally current, matched cart searches remain faster than shelf searches.
openings.rival_prediction: The advantage disappears after matching load and recency; the original sample reflects easier encounters.
openings.defeat: Matched cart searches are no faster, or cart capacity prevents equivalent loads.
openings.probe: Only if preparation capacity remains, alternate matched paper-timed retrieval rehearsals on the existing cart and shelves; restore locations and include restoration time.
assumptions: Available cart capacity and clerk preparation time permit the comparison.

evidence.decision: Start with T1 only after establishing remaining preparation capacity. Synthetic stipulations justify competing predictions, not benefits. Certainty alone cannot establish correct prompt pickup or the 95% target; neither eventual intervention is proven.

unresolved.issue: Cause of second searches and time cost of updates.

openings.claim: Location uncertainty is a plausible contributor to delayed correct-hold pickups, but the synthetic stipulations do not establish its cause or justify continuous location upkeep.
openings.delta: Prioritize a bounded cause-discrimination probe before choosing availability messaging, record upkeep, or cart storage as the intervention.
openings.prediction: Delayed encounters will disproportionately include stale location entries or household-name mismatches, including outside the concentrated demand interval.
openings.rival_prediction: Peak demand is the main driver: pickups with accurate locations will still exceed two minutes during the concentrated interval, while second searches explain little delay after accounting for waiting.
openings.defeat: Encounter-linked records show that stale locations and household-name mismatches rarely explain second searches or excess time, while accurate-location pickups remain delayed chiefly by waiting.
openings.probe: The existing clerk uses the existing timing sheet behind the desk to sample ordinary pickups, distinguishing waiting from retrieval time and noting second-search reason, location accuracy, arrival recency, and cart load. Verify the correct reader before every handoff. Use only the existing shelves, cart, paper, and pencils. Cap all daily preparation and upkeep at ten clerk-minutes; stop optional recording when that cap cannot be maintained. Evaluate diagnostic feasibility and association, not intervention efficacy.
assumptions: The clerk can capture sufficiently informative encounter notes within remaining preparation capacity without materially slowing handoffs.
The sample includes enough variation in demand and storage conditions to distinguish the rival explanations.

evidence.decision: Converge on bounded diagnosis as the next step. Its feasibility remains unverified; no eventual intervention is established. Preserve prompt, correct, private pickup for readers and the evening clerk, and retain the 95% within-two-minutes target with no wrong-reader handoffs.

unresolved.issue: Availability certainty may matter, but interview representativeness and any benefit remain unverified.
Cart speed may reflect recency or load; it does not establish a storage advantage.
Eight preparation minutes plus six correction minutes do not demonstrate compliance with the ten-minute allowance.

families.signature: Preparation defects may shift work into opening hours. Corrections should follow mismatches or obsolete location records and consume clerk time otherwise available for handoffs, potentially lengthening subsequent waits.
families.assumptions: Diary corrections are relevant to holds. Their causes and overlap with peak demand are unknown; whether all corrections count as daily preparation is not specified.

families.signature: Uncertainty about availability may increase perceived burden independently of physical retrieval time. Readers with equally long encounters could report different dissatisfaction according to whether they knew the hold was present.
families.assumptions: Interview statements reflect experience, but eight delayed readers may be unrepresentative. Reduced uncertainty alone would not establish the two-minute target or correct handoff.

openings.claim: Location upkeep deserves priority only if stale locations explain second searches and a correction fits the ten-minute preparation budget. Availability uncertainty may be an independent burden; these concerns need not conflict causally.
openings.delta: Replace competing priority assertions with a short event trace linking delay, verified location error, availability-answer timing, and correction cost before selecting an intervention.
openings.prediction: If stale exception locations are the actionable bottleneck, second searches will follow a specific obsolete entry, and correcting that entry will avoid a demonstrable search step at an affordable measured cost.
openings.rival_prediction: The nearest alternative is peak-window congestion with availability uncertainty: delayed encounters will have correct initial locations, cluster in the busy interval, and receive verified availability answers late. Location upkeep then leaves the principal delay intact.
openings.defeat: A trace showing correct initial locations throughout delayed encounters, with waiting dominating retrieval, defeats the proposed priority for stale-location upkeep in that observed batch.
openings.probe: Trace the next four delayed available-hold encounters using the existing timing sheet: queue wait, first and actual locations, obsolete slip or household-name mismatch, second-search duration, and first verified availability answer. After handoff, optionally ask which burden mattered most. Time one necessary entry correction only while total daily preparation, including corrections, remains below ten minutes; stop preparation at the cap. Keep all notes behind the desk and retain clerk-only handoffs. This is a diagnostic probe, not a tested intervention.
assumptions: The clerk can record the trace without materially delaying subsequent readers.
A necessary correction and its timing can fit within the remaining preparation allowance.
Four delayed encounters occur; their answers do not establish representativeness.

evidence.decision: Propose the bounded trace before choosing upkeep or an availability-response change. All supplied observations are synthetic stipulations; no benefit, agreement, causal effect, or 95-percent success rate is established.

unresolved.issue: The trace can identify plausible wasted steps but cannot prove either intervention improves outcomes.
Fast cart pickups remain confounded by recency, volume and size; do not choose cart storage from this sample.

openings.claim: Unreliable storage addresses plausibly contribute to delayed pickups, but their contribution and affordable upkeep are unproven. Evaluate a bounded diagnostic probe before choosing an intervention.
openings.delta: Link encounter time to address accuracy instead of inferring causation from separate timing, shelf and exception samples; retain cart storage as an unresolved option.
openings.prediction: Second-location delays disproportionately coincide with stale exception entries or household-name mismatches, including outside the demand burst.
openings.rival_prediction: Demand concentration principally causes delays, while cart pickups are selectively easy; accurately addressed pickups still exceed two minutes mainly during the concentrated interval.
openings.defeat: A linked sample showing accurate exception locations and correct surname placement in most second-location delays, with delays instead tracking congestion, would defeat prioritizing address repair.
openings.probe: During routine pickups, the existing clerk adds brief address-error and peak-interval marks to the existing behind-desk timing sheet. Keep names and contact details behind the desk, retain the two shelves and cart, and keep all daily preparation, including probe preparation and correction work, within ten clerk-minutes. Stop additional recording at that budget; insufficient coverage yields no conclusion. Maintain identity checks and record wrong-reader handoffs. Compare delay patterns without claiming tested improvement.
assumptions: Enough linked observations can be captured within the preparation cap without materially slowing handoffs.
The clerk can distinguish address failures from congestion during ordinary retrieval.

evidence.decision: Converge on this constrained diagnostic next step, not an established cause or effective intervention. Its design preserves constraints; meeting 95% within two minutes with no wrong-reader handoffs remains unproven. Availability certainty may help readers but cannot replace correct, private, prompt pickup.

unresolved.issue: Address errors have not been linked to the delayed encounters; upkeep cost remains unknown.
Cart comparability and interview representativeness remain unsettled; all observations are synthetic stipulations.

limits: Method labels are hidden; semantic content may remain recognizable.
